title: String Compression
description: Brute force to optimized: a separate result array versus in place two pointer compression.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of characters chars, compress it in place by replacing every run of repeated characters with the character followed by its count (a count of 1 is written as just the character alone, with no digit). Return the new length of the compressed array.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","A read pointer that identifies each run, and a write pointer that places the compressed result directly back into the same array."],["Difficulty","Intermediate"],["Tags","Strings, Two Pointers"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that compression never increases length, which guarantees the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer, making in place writing safe."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an array of characters chars, compress it in place by replacing every run of repeated characters with the character followed by its count (a count of 1 is written as just the character alone, with no digit). Return the new length of the compressed array.

blocks.title: Analogy: Shorthand for Counting Repeated Items
blocks.text: Like writing "5 apples" instead of listing "apple apple apple apple apple" five separate times, a natural shorthand for describing a run of identical items using just the item and how many there are.

blocks.caption: Every run of repeated characters becomes just the character followed by its count

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: chars = ["a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Run of 2 a's, run of 2 b's, run of 3 c's","compress each run as character plus digit count","each distinct consecutive run is replaced independently"],["Answer","[\"a\",\"2\",\"b\",\"2\",\"c\",\"3\"], new length 6","three runs, each contributing a letter and a digit, gives 6 total characters"]]}

blocks.text: Example: chars = ["a"]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A single character run of length 1 needs no digit at all","stays as just \"a\"","a count of 1 is represented by the character alone, per the problem's own rule"],["Answer","[\"a\"], new length 1","the array is already in its shortest compressed form"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: a run of 12 identical characters
A run whose count is 12 needs two separate digit characters, "1" and "2", written one after another, since the count itself can be multiple digits, giving for example ["b", "1", "2"] for twelve b's.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether the compressed result genuinely needs its own separate storage, or can safely be written back into the same array it came from.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Move Zeroes and the space compaction step of Reverse Words in a String already showed the read pointer, write pointer technique: scan forward with one pointer, and only ever write forward with a second, independent pointer.

Observation 2: The brute force builds an entirely separate result array and copies it back afterward, which produces the correct values but defeats the point of an in place solution.

Observation 3: The key fact that makes writing directly back into the same array safe is that compression never increases length, a run of 2 or more identical characters always produces fewer output characters than input characters consumed, and a run of exactly 1 produces exactly the same single character.

Observation 4: Because of that guarantee, the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer, so a read pointer that identifies each run and a write pointer that places the character and its digit count directly into the same array is always safe, confirmed by tracing chars equal to ["a","a","b","b","c","c","c"] through to the correct compressed length, 6.

Recognizing that compression can never make the array longer, only shorter or the same length, is what guarantees the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer, making a fully in place solution safe.
6. Brute Force Solution

Scan through the array once, building a completely separate new array containing every character followed by its run length as digit characters, then copy that new array back over the original in a second pass.
Step by step algorithm

items: Scan the array, identifying each run of identical consecutive characters.
For each run, append the character and its count (as separate digit characters if needed) to a new, separate array.
Copy the new array back over the original chars array.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A separate result list is built first, keeping the logic for identifying runs and formatting counts completely independent from any concerns about safely writing back into the original array.
A multi digit count is broken into its individual digit characters, since each digit occupies its own separate array position.
The original array is only overwritten after the entire compressed result is already known, in a distinct final copying pass.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every run is correctly identified and replaced with the character plus its digit count, so the compression is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to build the result plus one pass to copy it back.
Space: O(n), for the separate result list, which the problem explicitly wants to avoid.

Limitation: the problem asks for the compression to happen in place, using only O(1) extra space, but building an entirely separate result array first defeats that requirement even though the final values end up correct.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it builds a full separate array purely out of caution, even though nothing about the compressed result actually requires extra storage.

What guarantees in place writing is safe: a run of 2 or more characters always compresses to fewer characters than it consumed, and a run of 1 compresses to exactly the same single character, so the output position can never race ahead of the input position.

What that guarantee unlocks directly: a write pointer can safely lag at or behind the read pointer at all times, writing the compressed character and its digits directly into positions the read pointer has already passed.

The core idea: one read pointer identifies each run's character and length, one write pointer places the compressed result directly into the same array, with no separate storage needed at all.

Since the compressed output can never be longer than the original array (a run of 2 or more identical characters always shrinks when compressed, and a run of exactly 1 character stays exactly the same length), the compressed result can always be written directly back into the very same array, safely staying at or behind the original read position. Use a "read" pointer that scans through runs, and a separate "write" pointer that places the compressed character and its digit characters directly into the same array as it goes.
9. Optimized Solution
Two pointers: a read pointer identifying each run, and a write pointer placing the compressed result directly into the same array.
Dry run for chars = ["a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Run found","Written to array","Write pointer after"],"rows":[["\"a\" x2","a, 2","2"],["\"b\" x2","b, 2","4"],["\"c\" x3","c, 3","6"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a read pointer finds each run, a write pointer places the result in the same array

codes.python:
def compress(chars):
    write = 0
    read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        ch = chars[read]
        count = 0
        while read < n and chars[read] == ch:
            count += 1
            read += 1
        chars[write] = ch                                        # write the character directly in place
        write += 1
        if count > 1:
            for digit in str(count):
                chars[write] = digit                                  # write each digit character directly in place
                write += 1
    return write


if __name__ == "__main__":
    chars = ["a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c", "c"]
    new_length = compress(chars)
    print(new_length, chars[:new_length])

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the read pointer, by the time it finishes counting a run, is always at least as far ahead as the write pointer will ever need to reach for that run's compressed output, so writing the character and its digit characters directly at the write pointer's current position never overwrites data the read pointer has not already consumed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A run has a count of exactly 1","Only the character itself is written, no digit","The write pointer advances by exactly the same amount the read pointer did for this run"],["A run has a count of 2 or more","The character plus each digit of its count is written","The write pointer advances by strictly less than the read pointer did, guaranteeing it never catches up or overtakes"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass, since read never falls behind write.
Space: O(1) extra, the array is compressed directly in place.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The key correctness fact that makes the in place two pointer approach safe is that the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer, since compressing a run of length 2 or more always produces fewer characters than the run itself, and a run of exactly 1 produces the same single character.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing the count as a single character when it is 10 or greater, instead of writing each digit of the count separately.
Forgetting to skip writing any digits at all when a run has a count of exactly 1.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single character array","Compresses to itself unchanged."],["A run with a count of 10 or more","Needs multiple digit characters written one after another."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
State clearly why the in place approach is safe before writing any code: the write pointer position can never exceed the read pointer position, since compression never increases length.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: a read pointer for runs, a write pointer for the compressed output, directly into the same array.
If the interviewer says "why is writing back into the same array safe here", think: compression never increases length, so the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer.
If the interviewer says "what about counts of 10 or more", think: write each digit of the count as its own separate character.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why can the write pointer never overtake the read pointer during this compression?
How would you decompress a compressed array back into its original repeated form?
How would this approach change if runs could wrap around the array, treating it as circular?
How would you compress the array if counts needed to be written in a fixed width, zero padded format instead of variable length digits?
How would you adapt this approach to compress based on runs of identical adjacent elements in a general array, not just characters?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Move Zeroes, whose read and write pointer compaction is the direct ancestor of the technique used here.
Reverse Words in a String, whose final space-compaction pass uses this exact same read pointer, write pointer idea to collapse extra spaces in place.
Any "condense or filter a sequence in place" problem, where proving the output can never be longer than the input is the key step that justifies writing directly back into the same storage.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a read pointer that identifies each run, and a write pointer that places the compressed result directly back into the same array.

Core Idea: compression never increases length, so the write pointer can never overtake the read pointer, which guarantees writing the compressed result directly back into the same array is always safe.
Time: O(n) for both approaches.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's separate result array, O(1) extra for the optimized in place approach.
Most Important Observation: proving the output can never outgrow the input is precisely what justifies skipping a separate result array entirely.
Interview Difficulty: the two pointer idea itself is standard; correctly handling multi digit counts and count-of-1 runs is where implementation bugs tend to appear.
One line memory trick: read a whole run, write its character and digit count directly back, the write pointer can never catch the read pointer.
